decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All flat-head fasteners on the shelf are screws.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premise about flat heads only addresses screws. Bolts may also have flat heads — nothing in the data rules this out.

title: Coffee Roastery Beans
stem:
A roastery sorts 60 batches of beans by three labels. 24 are single origin, 20 are decaffeinated and 22 are organic. 7 batches are both single origin and decaffeinated, 8 are both single origin and organic, and 6 are both decaffeinated and organic. 3 batches carry all three labels. 12 batches do not fall under any of these labels.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies from the stem: 3 batches sit in the centre (all three labels) and 12 sit outside any label. Scan the options. B shows 5 in the centre — eliminate B. C shows 9 outside — eliminate C. That leaves A and D. The decaffeinated-and-organic-only region equals 6 minus the 3 that also have single origin = 3. D shows 6 there (it forgot to subtract the triple) — eliminate D. A shows 3 — correct.

title: Veterinary Practice Add-ons
stem:
A veterinary practice records 70 ongoing treatments. 30 cases involve diabetes. Of those, 14 also include daily insulin, 8 also include a renal supplement and 6 also include a weight management plan. None of the diabetes cases involves more than one of these add-ons. 12 cases involve daily insulin without a diabetes diagnosis, 10 cases involve a renal supplement without a diabetes diagnosis, and 8 cases involve a weight management plan without a diabetes diagnosis. 10 cases are in none of these four categories.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies from the stem: 14 cases sit in the diabetes-and-insulin lens, 8 in the diabetes-and-renal lens, 6 in the diabetes-and-weight lens, and 10 are outside. Scan the options. B shows 12 in the diabetes-and-insulin lens — eliminate B. C shows 8 outside — eliminate C. That leaves A and D. Diabetes only (no add-on) = 30 − 14 − 8 − 6 = 2. D shows 12 there (it forgot to subtract the three add-ons) — eliminate D. A shows 2 — correct.

title: Craft School Modules
stem:
The diagram shows 240 attendees of a craft school programme, categorised by their hands-on workshop attendance and the specific modules in which they are enrolled. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents an attendee enrolled in module B and module C, but not in module A and not in the online-theory programme?
answer_reason: The question wants module B and module C, with no module A and no online-theory enrolment — so inside the Hands-on workshop, inside both Module B and Module C, outside Module A and outside the Online-theory shape. Letter T sits in Hands-on with Module A and Module B — includes Module A, which is excluded. Letter S is Hands-on with Module C only — missing Module B. Letter V is Online theory only — missing the workshop and the modules entirely. Letter U sits inside Hands-on with both Module B and Module C, outside Module A and outside Online theory — that is the region we want.

title: Hospital Patient Cohort
stem:
The diagram shows 300 patients on a long-term care ward, categorised by five health attributes. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a patient who is on statins and diabetic, but is not over 65, hypertensive, or a smoker?
answer_reason: The question wants a patient inside both On statins and Diabetic, but outside Over 65, Hypertensive and Smoker. Letter X is Over 65 and On statins — includes Over 65, which is excluded. Letter U is Diabetic and Hypertensive — includes Hypertensive. Letter T is On statins only — missing Diabetic. Letter Y sits in the overlap of On statins and Diabetic, outside the other three shapes — that is the region we want.

title: Tool Hire Yard Stock
stem:
A tool hire yard has 80 powered hand tools in stock. All cordless tools at the yard are battery-powered. All brushless-motor tools at the yard are cordless. 28 of the powered hand tools are battery-powered. 22 of the powered hand tools are cordless. 9 of the powered hand tools have brushless motors.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies from the stem: 9 tools are brushless and 80 − 28 = 52 are not battery-powered (the outside region). Scan the options. B shows 11 in the brushless centre — eliminate B. D shows 60 outside — eliminate D. That leaves A and C. The cordless ring should be cordless minus brushless = 22 − 9 = 13. C shows 22 in that ring — that is the full cordless total, so it double-counts the brushless tools — eliminate C. A shows 13 — correct.

title: Spinner Sums
stem:
A fair spinner is divided into eight equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. The spinner is spun twice and the two results are recorded.

What is the probability that the sum of the two spins is greater than 12?
answer_reason: There are 8 × 8 = 64 equally likely outcomes. Pairs (a, b) with a + b > 12: sum 13 has (5,8), (6,7), (7,6), (8,5) = 4; sum 14 has (6,8), (7,7), (8,6) = 3; sum 15 has (7,8), (8,7) = 2; sum 16 has (8,8) = 1. Total favourable = 10. Probability = 10 / 64 = 5/32.

title: Drug Screening Test
stem:
A workplace drug screening test has the following properties. When a worker has used the substance, the test correctly returns positive 96% of the time. When a worker has not used the substance, the test correctly returns negative 88% of the time. In a workforce of 5,000 workers, 250 have actually used the substance. A randomly chosen worker tests positive.

Approximately what is the probability that this worker has actually used the substance?
answer_reason: Of 5,000 workers, 250 are users and 4,750 are non-users. True positives = 96% × 250 = 240. False positives = 12% × 4,750 = 570. Total positives = 240 + 570 = 810. Probability of being a user given a positive test = 240 / 810 ≈ 0.296, so about 30%.

title: Charity Lottery Tickets
stem:
A small charity lottery sells 600 tickets numbered 1 to 600. One winning ticket is drawn at random. The prize is awarded to any ticket whose number is divisible by exactly one of 4 or 5 (but not both).

What is the probability that the drawn ticket wins the prize?
answer_reason: Numbers from 1 to 600 divisible by 4: 600 / 4 = 150. Divisible by 5: 600 / 5 = 120. Divisible by both 4 and 5 (i.e. by 20): 600 / 20 = 30. Divisible by exactly one of 4 or 5 = (150 − 30) + (120 − 30) = 120 + 90 = 210. Probability = 210 / 600 = 7/20.

title: Penalty Shoot-out
stem:
A footballer scores from a penalty kick with probability 0.8 on each attempt, independently of other attempts. The footballer takes three penalty kicks in a competition shoot-out.

What is the probability that the footballer scores at least one of the three penalties?
answer_reason: P(misses all three) = 0.2 × 0.2 × 0.2 = 0.008. P(scores at least one) = 1 − 0.008 = 0.992.

title: Two Cards Different Suits
stem:
A standard pack of 52 playing cards is shuffled. Two cards are drawn one after another, without replacement.

What is the probability that the two cards are of different suits?
answer_reason: After the first card is drawn, 51 cards remain. Of those, 12 share the first card's suit and 39 do not. P(different suits) = 39 / 51 = 13/17.

title: Train Conductors and Uniforms
stem: All train conductors wear blue uniforms. Some blue uniforms are fleeces. No fleece carries a shoulder badge. All shoulder badges bear a reference number.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some train conductors wear fleeces.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Conductors wear blue uniforms and some blue uniforms are fleeces — but conductors could all be wearing the non-fleece kind of blue uniform. We cannot deduce any conductor wears a fleece.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A train conductor wearing a fleece cannot carry a shoulder badge.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: If a conductor is wearing a fleece, they are wearing a fleece — and no fleece carries a shoulder badge.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every reference number appears on a shoulder badge.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. All shoulder badges bear a reference number, but we cannot conclude that all reference numbers are on badges — reference numbers could exist elsewhere.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some blue uniforms are not fleeces.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: In UCAT, 'some' means strictly more than 0 and less than 100 per cent. So some blue uniforms being fleeces guarantees some blue uniforms are not fleeces.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All train conductors carry a shoulder badge.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises never say conductors carry shoulder badges. We cannot add this from outside knowledge.

title: Zemmers and Wabbles
stem: All zemmers are prilks. All prilks are kloffs. Some kloffs are blargs. No blarg is a wabble.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All zemmers are kloffs.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every zemmer is a prilk, and every prilk is a kloff — so every zemmer is a kloff.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some zemmers are blargs.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Zemmers are kloffs, and some kloffs are blargs — but zemmers could be among the kloffs that are not blargs. Multiple 'some' claims do not chain.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No zemmer is a wabble.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We have no information about zemmers and wabbles. Zemmers are kloffs, and wabbles are excluded only from blargs — zemmers could still be wabbles.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All kloffs are zemmers.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. 'All zemmers are kloffs' does not mean 'all kloffs are zemmers' — there may be kloffs that are neither zemmers nor prilks.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some kloffs are not wabbles.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Some kloffs are blargs, and no blarg is a wabble. So those blarg-kloffs are not wabbles, which means some kloffs are not wabbles.

title: Research Wing Access
stem: A security badge permits entry to the research wing unless it has been deactivated. Every deactivated badge is logged in the visitor system. Only staff members are issued permanent badges. Badges that are not permanent expire within 24 hours.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A staff member's badge always permits entry to the research wing.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: A staff member's badge could be deactivated, in which case it does not permit entry. Being a staff member doesn't override deactivation.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: If a badge is not logged in the visitor system, it has not been deactivated.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every deactivated badge is logged — the contrapositive is: if not logged, then not deactivated.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every badge in the visitor system is deactivated.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. We know deactivated badges are logged, but the visitor system could log non-deactivated badges too.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A person who is not a staff member cannot hold a permanent badge.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 'Only staff members are issued permanent badges' means if a badge is permanent, its holder is a staff member. Non-staff therefore cannot have a permanent badge.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every badge that expires within 24 hours belongs to a non-staff member.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Non-permanent badges expire within 24 hours, but the premises don't stop staff members from holding non-permanent badges. So a short-life badge could still belong to a staff member.

title: Keys, Inspections and Certificates
stem: A working key is necessary to start the engine. Passing the safety inspection is sufficient to obtain a roadworthiness certificate. Every roadworthiness certificate expires 12 months after issue.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: If an engine has started, a working key was used.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: A necessary condition must be met for the outcome to occur. Engine started → a working key was used.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A car that passes the safety inspection is issued a roadworthiness certificate.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 'Passing is sufficient' means passing guarantees the certificate.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Having a working key is sufficient to start the engine.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premise only says a working key is necessary — other factors (fuel, battery, ignition switch) may also be required. Necessary is not the same as sufficient.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A roadworthiness certificate issued 18 months ago is still valid.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Certificates expire after 12 months, so an 18-month-old certificate has expired.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A car that fails the safety inspection cannot receive a roadworthiness certificate.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Passing is sufficient, but the premises don't say it is the only route. There could be another path to the certificate, so failure isn't guaranteed to block it.

title: Climbing Peak Bourn
stem: Only members of the alpine club may climb peak Bourn. No one climbs peak Bourn without a registered helmet. Some registered helmets are older than ten years. Any helmet older than ten years must be inspected annually.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Everyone who climbs peak Bourn is a member of the alpine club.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 'Only X may do Y' means doing Y requires being X. Anyone climbing the peak must be a club member.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every alpine club member has climbed peak Bourn.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. Being a member permits climbing but doesn't force it.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Anyone who climbs peak Bourn has a registered helmet.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: No one climbs without one, so climbing implies having a registered helmet.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some alpine club members own helmets older than ten years.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We know some registered helmets are that old, but those helmets need not belong to alpine club members — the premises don't link the two groups.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every registered helmet must be inspected annually.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only helmets older than ten years must be inspected — and only 'some' registered helmets are that old. Newer registered helmets are not covered.

title: Quiz Show Finish
stem:
Five contestants — Aditi, Beth, Carl, Dina and Ed — finished a quiz show in positions 1 to 5 (1 = first, 5 = last). Dina finished ahead of Carl but behind Beth. Aditi finished ahead of Beth. Ed finished exactly one position behind Carl. Carl did not finish last.

Who finished second?
answer_reason: Aditi is ahead of Beth, who is ahead of Dina, who is ahead of Carl. Ed is one position behind Carl, and Carl is not last, so Carl must be fourth and Ed fifth. That fixes Aditi first, Beth second, Dina third. Beth finished second.

title: Neighbours, Houses and Cars
stem:
Four neighbours — Anna, Ben, Carla and Dev — live in houses numbered 1 to 4 on one side of a street, each in a different house. Each drives a different car: saloon, SUV, hatchback or estate. Carla lives exactly two houses from Ben. The SUV is parked at house 2. The hatchback is parked at an odd-numbered house. Dev's house number is higher than the hatchback driver's. Anna drives the estate. Ben drives the saloon.

Who lives at house 3?
answer_reason: Anna drives the estate, so Anna is not at house 2 (the SUV) and not at the hatchback house. The hatchback is at an odd house, and Dev is to its right, so the hatchback is at house 1 and Dev is at 2, 3 or 4. Testing positions: Anna must be at house 4. The remaining houses 1 and 3 belong to Carla and Ben, who are two apart (checks). Ben drives the saloon so Ben is not at house 1 (the hatchback) — Ben is at house 3. Carla takes house 1 with the hatchback. Dev is at house 2 with the SUV.

title: Charity Shop Tiers
stem:
A charity shop sold 40 items one day. Five items sold at £20 each. Twelve items sold at £5 each. The remaining items were split between a £3 tier and a £12 tier, with exactly three more items at the £3 tier than at the £12 tier.

How many items sold at the £3 tier?
answer_reason: After the £20 and £5 items, 40 − 5 − 12 = 23 items remain. Let the £12 count be y and the £3 count be y + 3. Then y + (y + 3) = 23, giving 2y = 20, so y = 10 and the £3 tier has y + 3 = 13 items.

title: Steering Committee Selection
stem:
A company is forming a five-person steering committee from four departments. Each department contributes people as listed below.

Sales: Rahul (M), Tom (M), Maya (F). Engineering: Ben (M), Lina (F), Priya (F). Finance: Dan (M), Sara (F). HR: Joy (F).

The committee must include at least one person from each department, at most two people from any single department, and exactly three men and two women. Sales and Engineering must together contribute exactly three people. Rahul will not be on the committee.

Who must definitely be on the committee?
answer_reason: HR has only Joy, so Joy is on. With Rahul out, Sales can contribute from {Tom, Maya}. If Sales contributes 2, both Tom and Maya are on; the remaining Engineering seat must be male (only Ben fits) and Finance must be male (Dan). If Sales contributes 1 (Tom, since Maya alone would force too many women), Engineering contributes 2 including Ben plus one of Lina/Priya, and Finance is Dan. In every valid configuration Ben is on the committee. Lina and Priya each appear in only one configuration; Sara never appears (Finance is always Dan).

title: Shared Office Theft
stem:
A theft occurred in a shared office. Three colleagues — Pat, Quinn and Rue — were present. Exactly one of them committed the theft and lied about it; the other two told the truth.

Pat said: "Rue took the money."
Quinn said: "I did not take the money."
Rue said: "Quinn is lying."

Who took the money?
answer_reason: Test each suspect as the thief-and-liar. If Pat is the thief, Pat's claim is false, so Rue didn't take it — but Rue's truthful claim is that Quinn is lying, contradicting Quinn's truthful denial. If Quinn is the thief, Quinn's claim 'I did not take it' is a lie (consistent), but Pat truthfully says Rue took it — contradiction. If Rue is the thief, Pat truthfully says Rue took it, Quinn truthfully denies taking it, and Rue's claim that Quinn is lying is false (consistent with Rue being the liar). All three statements are consistent only if Rue is the thief.

title: Mandatory Flu Vaccinations
stem: Should all hospital staff be required to receive annual flu vaccinations to reduce patient infection rates?
answer_reason: A is the strongest argument: it links the action (mandatory staff vaccination) to the outcome (patient infection rates) with trial data showing the intended effect. B addresses staff attitudes, not infection rates. C addresses staff autonomy, not the proposition's outcome. D uses 'some' and addresses staff availability, not patient infections.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a trial across three UK teaching hospitals found that wards with over 90 per cent staff vaccination recorded 35 per cent fewer patient flu cases than wards below 70 per cent.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; most nurses already feel morally obliged to protect their patients.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; mandating vaccinations removes individual staff choice.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some staff experience side effects that limit their working availability.

title: Four-Day School Week
stem: Should secondary schools introduce a four-day school week to improve student well-being?
answer_reason: A is the strongest: it addresses the action (four-day week) and the outcome (student well-being) with trial evidence of an 18 per cent fall in self-reported anxiety and no loss in academic results. B addresses teacher benefits, not student well-being. C addresses parental childcare, a separate outcome. D addresses perceived necessity — it neither measures well-being nor engages with whether the change would improve it.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; trials in two Scottish secondary schools reported student-reported anxiety scores fell 18 per cent after a four-day week was introduced, with no change in academic results.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; teachers will benefit from having an extra day off each week.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; parents with full-time jobs may struggle to arrange childcare for the extra day.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; students already have long summer breaks, so adding another day off is unnecessary.

title: Menu Calorie Labelling
stem: Should restaurants be required to display calorie information on menus to help customers make healthier choices?
answer_reason: A links the action (calorie labelling) to the outcome (healthier choices) with cross-country review evidence that average calorie intake per meal fell where labelling was mandatory. B is values-based with no evidence on healthier choices. C critiques the measure rather than the proposition — the limits of calories as a metric don't show labelling fails to influence choices. D uses vague 'many' and doesn't address whether those who do read labels make healthier choices.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a 2023 review of menu calorie labelling across 12 countries found average calorie intake per meal fell by 32 kcal where labelling was mandatory.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; transparency is a core value of modern hospitality.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; calorie counts alone don't capture the full nutritional quality of a meal.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; many customers ignore calorie labels entirely.

title: Quarterly Rainfall Stations
stem: The table shows the average rainfall (mm) recorded at four weather stations each quarter of one year.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Beacon recorded the highest rainfall of the four stations in Q4.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Q4 values: Alvin 95, Beacon 140, Cresta 70, Denny 75. Beacon is highest.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Cresta had a higher total annual rainfall than Alvin.
At every station, Q3 had higher rainfall than Q1.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Alvin Q3 (48) is below Q1 (85); Beacon Q3 (60) below Q1 (110); Denny Q3 (68) below Q1 (72). The claim fails.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Q1 receives more rain than any other quarter nationwide.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Four stations cannot be generalised to 'nationwide', and across them Q1 totals 317 mm while Q4 totals 380 mm.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Denny's rainfall in Q3 was the lowest across the four stations for that quarter.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Q3 values: Alvin 48, Beacon 60, Cresta 120, Denny 68. Alvin is the lowest, not Denny.

title: Puffin Populations Passage
stem: A marine research institute reports that between 2015 and 2023, puffin numbers on Island X declined by 22 per cent while on Island Y, where a predator-control programme was introduced in 2018, puffin numbers rose by 11 per cent over the same period. The institute argues the rise on Island Y shows predator control boosts puffin populations. Critics note Island Y also experienced unusually warm summers during those years, which tend to improve feeding conditions for puffins.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Predator control was responsible for the puffin rise on Island Y.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage presents this as the institute's argument, but critics cite warm summers as an alternative cause. The passage does not establish a causal link.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Puffin numbers on Island X fell between 2015 and 2023.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage states a 22 per cent decline on Island X over that period.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Introducing predator control will raise puffin populations on any island it is used on.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: A generalisation to 'any island' goes well beyond the mixed-cause rise described on one island.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Warm summers tend to improve feeding conditions for puffins.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage explicitly states this as a point made by critics.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Island X did not have a predator-control programme between 2015 and 2023.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage only states that Island Y had one. It does not state or imply the absence of such a programme on Island X.

title: Car Park Vehicles
stem: In a car park there are 60 vehicles, consisting only of estates and hatchbacks. 25 vehicles are electric and 35 are petrol. 20 vehicles are estates. 12 of the electric vehicles are estates. None of the petrol estates are white. Eight of the hatchbacks are white.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some petrol hatchbacks are white.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Eight hatchbacks are white, but the car park has 13 electric hatchbacks — the eight white hatchbacks could all be electric. We cannot deduce any petrol hatchbacks are white.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: The majority of white vehicles in the car park are hatchbacks.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We don't know the total number of white vehicles. No petrol estates are white, but electric estates could all be white, giving up to 12 white estates versus eight white hatchbacks.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every petrol estate is non-white.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Directly stated in the stem.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: There are 27 petrol hatchbacks in the car park.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Estates total 20, with 12 electric — so 8 are petrol estates. Petrol total is 35, so petrol hatchbacks = 35 − 8 = 27.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: If a vehicle is a non-white estate, it must be petrol.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Electric estates have no colour information — some could be non-white. So a non-white estate could be electric.

title: Homeware Product Revenue
stem: The table shows quarterly sales revenue (£ thousands) for three products at a homeware retailer.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Rugs generated more annual revenue than lamps and cushions combined.
Cushion sales grew by more than 50 per cent from Q1 to Q4.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Cushions rose from 45 to 75 — an increase of 30. 30 ÷ 45 ≈ 66.7 per cent, which is more than 50 per cent.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every product saw revenue fall between Q2 and Q3.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Rugs 135→110, Lamps 95→85, Cushions 60→50 — every product fell.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Lamps had a higher percentage growth from Q1 to Q4 than cushions did.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Lamps grew from 80 to 100 — a 25 per cent rise. Cushions grew by about 66.7 per cent. Cushions' growth is higher.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Cushion sales will reach £90,000 by Q5.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Extrapolation beyond the data provided. The table does not cover Q5, so future values cannot be deduced.

title: Low-Traffic Neighbourhoods
stem: A city council reports that since low-traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs) were introduced in 2021, air-pollution measurements on affected streets have fallen by 14 per cent on average. Residents' associations in some LTN areas note that traffic has shifted onto surrounding main roads, where pollution monitoring equipment recorded higher readings over the same period. The council maintains the policy has been a success overall, while acknowledging that 'pollution displacement' warrants further study.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Air pollution on streets affected by LTNs has fallen on average.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage states a 14 per cent average fall on LTN-affected streets.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: LTNs have reduced overall city-wide air pollution.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage describes a fall on LTN streets and a rise on surrounding main roads. The net city-wide effect is not given.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Traffic volumes on main roads in LTN areas increased after 2021.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage reports higher pollution readings on main roads, not traffic-volume measurements. Higher pollution does not confirm higher traffic.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: The council accepts that pollution displacement may have occurred.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage says the council acknowledges that pollution displacement warrants further study — this is an acceptance that the phenomenon may have occurred.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: LTNs should not be introduced in other cities.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage makes no recommendation about other cities and does not supply data that would justify one.

title: Summer Camp Activities
stem:
A summer camp has 80 children choosing three activities: archery, kayaking and rock climbing. 30 children do archery, 40 do kayaking and 25 do rock climbing. 12 children do both archery and kayaking. 10 children do both kayaking and rock climbing. No child does both archery and rock climbing. 7 children have not chosen an activity yet.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Two freebies: 7 children haven't chosen anything (outside) and no child does archery and rock climbing (so there is no archery-and-rock-climbing region in the correct diagram). Scan — B shows 12 in the archery-and-rock-climbing overlap, contradicting the stem — eliminate B. C shows only 4 outside — eliminate C. That leaves A and D. Archery total must be 30 = archery only + archery-and-kayaking = archery only + 12, so archery only = 18. A shows 18; D shows 14 — eliminate D. Answer: A.

title: After-School Club Wings
stem:
A secondary school runs after-school clubs in two separate wings of the building. The East Wing hosts chess and debate; the West Wing hosts football and drama. 100 students attend clubs overall. 13 students are in chess, 15 in debate, 18 in football and 21 in drama. 5 students are in both chess and debate. 6 students are in both football and drama. No student attends clubs in both wings. 44 students are not currently in any club.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Two freebies: 44 students are outside and the chess-and-debate overlap is 5. Scan — C shows 40 outside — eliminate C. D shows 3 in the chess-and-debate overlap — eliminate D. That leaves A and B. Football total must be 18 = football only + football-and-drama. A has 12 + 6 = 18 ✓. B has 10 + 8 = 18, but then drama only becomes 15 + 6 = 21 overall only if drama only = 13 — B shows 15, so drama total = 15 + 8 = 23, not 21. Eliminate B. Answer: A.

title: Unlabelled Office Desk Items
stem:
In a stationery company, 80 desks are surveyed. 40 have a lamp, 35 have a monitor and 30 have a plant. 15 desks have both a lamp and a monitor. 12 desks have both a lamp and a plant. 10 desks have both a monitor and a plant. 6 desks have all three items. 6 desks have none of these items.

Which of the following diagrams is consistent with the data?
answer_reason: Two freebies: 6 desks have all three items (the triple-overlap region) and 6 desks have none (the outside region). Scan — B shows 4 in the triple overlap — eliminate B. C shows 10 outside — eliminate C. That leaves A and D. Each shape must sum to its stated total (lamp 40, monitor 35, plant 30). In D, the three shape totals come out as 38, 37 and 30 — none matches lamp 40 or monitor 35. In A, the three shapes sum to 40, 35 and 30 as required, whichever shape you assign to which category. Answer: A.

title: Workplace Tool Library
stem:
The diagram categorises 150 apps in a workplace tool library by four attributes: communication, scheduling, analytics and security. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents an app that is both an analytics tool and a security tool, but is neither a communication nor a scheduling tool?
answer_reason: The question wants analytics and security, with communication and scheduling both excluded. Letter R is analytics only — no security. Letter U is scheduling and analytics — includes scheduling, which is excluded. Letter W is communication and security — includes communication, which is excluded. Letter V sits in the analytics-and-security overlap outside the other two — that is the region we want.

title: Hospital Patient Records
stem:
The diagram categorises 200 patient records at a hospital by five attributes: inpatient, on medication, has allergy note, requires interpreter and flagged for follow-up. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents an inpatient who requires an interpreter but has no allergy note, is not on medication and is not flagged for follow-up?
answer_reason: The question needs a record that is inpatient and requires interpreter, but outside the medication, allergy-note and follow-up sets. Letter Q is inpatient and on medication — includes medication, excluded. Letter R is inpatient and has an allergy note — excluded. Letter W is requires interpreter only and sits outside inpatient. Letter S is inside inpatient and requires interpreter, and outside all three excluded sets — that is the region we want.

title: Company Training Modules
stem:
The diagram categorises 100 training modules at a company by three attributes: technical, compliance and advanced. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a module that is both technical and compliance but is not advanced?
answer_reason: Letter P is technical only — not in compliance. Letter Q is compliance only — not in technical. Letter S sits inside all three shapes — includes advanced, which is excluded. Letter R is inside both technical and compliance and outside advanced — that is the region we want.

title: Marbles in a Bag
stem:
A bag contains 5 green marbles, 7 yellow marbles and 8 blue marbles. One marble is drawn at random.

What is the probability that the marble drawn is not blue?
answer_reason: Total marbles = 5 + 7 + 8 = 20. Non-blue marbles = 5 + 7 = 12. P(not blue) = 12 / 20 = 3/5.

title: Cycling Commute Survey
stem:
A survey of 300 people asked whether they cycle to work. 120 respondents are under 30, and 60 of these under-30s cycle. 180 respondents are 30 or older, and 36 of these cycle. One respondent is chosen at random from those who cycle.

What is the probability they are under 30?
answer_reason: Total cyclists = 60 + 36 = 96. Under-30 cyclists = 60. P(under 30 | cycles) = 60 / 96 = 5/8.

title: Weighing Scales Comparison
stem:
Two weighing scales are tested. Scale 1 gives the correct weight in 88 out of 100 trials; when used 50 times on the same object, it returns the same reading 47 times. Scale 2 gives the correct weight in 94 out of 100 trials; when used 50 times on the same object, it returns the same reading 42 times.

Accuracy is how often a scale gives the correct reading; precision is how consistently it gives the same reading on repeated use. Which statement best compares the two scales?
answer_reason: Scale 1: accuracy 88/100 = 88 per cent; precision 47/50 = 94 per cent. Scale 2: accuracy 94/100 = 94 per cent; precision 42/50 = 84 per cent. So Scale 2 is more accurate but Scale 1 is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Scale 1 is more accurate but Scale 2 is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Scale 2 is both more accurate and more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Scale 2 is more accurate but Scale 1 is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Scale 1 is both more accurate and more precise.

title: Two Dice Rolls
stem:
A board game turn requires rolling a single fair six-sided die twice. A player wins extra points if they roll a 6 on the first roll AND an even number on the second roll. The two rolls are independent.

What is the probability of winning extra points?
answer_reason: P(6 on first roll) = 1/6. P(even on second roll) = 3/6 = 1/2. Independent events multiply: 1/6 × 1/2 = 1/12.

title: Parcel Inspection
stem: A parcel can be delivered to a customer unless it has been flagged for inspection. All parcels flagged for inspection are held at the depot. Only senior officers may release a parcel held at the depot.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A parcel that has not been flagged for inspection may be delivered to a customer.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 'X unless Y' means X is true except when Y. A parcel can be delivered unless flagged — so a parcel that has not been flagged may be delivered.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every parcel held at the depot has been flagged for inspection.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. The stem says all flagged parcels are held at the depot, not that every held parcel is flagged. Parcels could be held at the depot for other reasons.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No parcel anywhere can be released except by a senior officer.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Scope creep. The premise restricts only release of parcels held at the depot to senior officers. It says nothing about parcels elsewhere.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A junior officer cannot release a parcel held at the depot.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only senior officers may release depot-held parcels, so any non-senior officer, including juniors, cannot.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some parcels flagged for inspection are not held at the depot.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: All parcels flagged for inspection are held at the depot — directly contradicts the conclusion.

title: Blorps and Crindles
stem: All blorps are crindles. Some crindles are dweelies. No dweelie is a flump. Every flump is a crindle.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All blorps are crindles.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Directly stated in the premises.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some blorps are dweelies.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Blorps are crindles, and some crindles are dweelies — but the dweelie crindles are not guaranteed to include any blorps. Two chained 'some' claims do not combine.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No blorp is a flump.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Blorps are crindles and flumps are crindles, but the premises do not forbid a blorp from also being a flump. Cannot be concluded.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some crindles are not dweelies.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: In UCAT, 'some' means strictly more than 0% and strictly less than 100%. So 'some crindles are dweelies' means some are and some are not.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every flump is a dweelie.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises state no dweelie is a flump — so flumps and dweelies are mutually exclusive. The conclusion directly contradicts this.

title: Distinction Grade
stem: If a student completes the research essay, they qualify for the distinction grade. Passing all four end-of-year exams is necessary for qualifying for the distinction grade. Gemma qualified for the distinction grade this year.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Gemma passed all four end-of-year exams.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Passing all four exams is necessary for distinction; Gemma qualified for distinction, so she must have passed all four.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Gemma completed the research essay.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The essay is sufficient for qualifying but not stated to be necessary. Gemma might have qualified another way, without the essay.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Any student who passes all four end-of-year exams qualifies for the distinction grade.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Passing all four is necessary for distinction, but not stated to be sufficient. Other requirements could also apply.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A student who did not pass all four end-of-year exams cannot qualify for the distinction grade.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The contrapositive of 'passing all four is necessary for distinction' is 'if not all four passed, then no distinction'.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every student who completes the research essay passes all four end-of-year exams.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Completing the essay implies distinction, and distinction requires all four exams — so essay completion chains to all four exams passed.

title: Hospital Surgeons
stem: All senior surgeons at the hospital trained in London. Some surgeons at the hospital are senior. Most surgeons who trained in London studied at King's College. No junior surgeon leads a transplant team.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All senior surgeons at the hospital studied at King's College.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Seniors all trained in London, and most London-trained surgeons studied at King's — but 'most' is not 'all'. Seniors could be among the minority who trained elsewhere in London.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: At least some surgeons at the hospital trained in London.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Some surgeons are senior, and all senior surgeons trained in London — so at least some surgeons trained in London.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No senior surgeon leads a transplant team.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premise rules out junior surgeons leading transplant teams. It says nothing about seniors.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every surgeon who leads a transplant team must be a senior surgeon.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Ruling out juniors does not restrict transplant leaders to seniors — other grades (registrars, consultants) could also lead.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A junior surgeon does not lead a transplant team.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Directly stated in the premises.

title: Circular Dinner Seating
stem:
Six friends — Alice, Ben, Carla, Dan, Evie, Finn — sit in six numbered seats arranged clockwise around a circular table (seats 1 to 6, with seat 1 next to seats 2 and 6, and directly opposite seat 4). Alice sits in seat 2. Dan sits directly opposite Alice. Ben sits immediately clockwise of Alice. Carla sits immediately clockwise of Dan. Finn does not sit next to Ben.

Who sits in seat 4?
answer_reason: Alice is in seat 2, so Dan is in seat 5 (opposite). Ben is immediately clockwise of Alice = seat 3. Carla is immediately clockwise of Dan = seat 6. Seats 1 and 4 remain for Evie and Finn. Finn cannot sit next to Ben (seat 3); the seats next to seat 3 are 2 (Alice) and 4. So Finn cannot take seat 4 — Finn is in seat 1 and Evie is in seat 4.

title: Sibling Ages
stem:
Four siblings — Alex, Ben, Cora and Dina — have a combined age of 81 years. Alex is three years younger than Ben. Cora is twice Dina's age. Dina is four years younger than Alex.

How old is Dina?
answer_reason: Let Dina = D. Then Alex = D + 4, Ben = Alex + 3 = D + 7, Cora = 2D. Sum: D + (D + 4) + (D + 7) + 2D = 5D + 11 = 81, so 5D = 70 and D = 14.

title: Colleague Cars
stem:
Five office colleagues — Noah, Olivia, Priya, Quinn, Riya — each drive a different-coloured car: red, blue, green, silver, or black. Quinn drives the green car. Priya drives either the silver or the red car. Noah does not drive the red or the blue car. Olivia drives the blue car. Riya drives the red car.

Which colour does Noah drive?
answer_reason: Quinn takes green, Olivia takes blue, Riya takes red. Priya drives silver or red, and red is Riya's — so Priya drives silver. Noah cannot drive red or blue, and green, silver, and red are taken — Noah drives black.

title: Charity Volunteer Team
stem:
A company's five departments offered volunteers for a 20-person charity event. The team must have exactly 4 volunteers from each department, with an equal split of 2 men and 2 women per department. 22 people volunteered, shown in the table below by department and gender.

For the department where more volunteers came forward than needed spots, those volunteers will be interviewed before the final team is selected.

Which volunteers will take part in the interview?
answer_reason: Each department needs 2 men and 2 women. Sales, IT, HR and Design each have exactly 2 men and 2 women — all selected automatically. Marketing has 2 men (automatically selected) but 3 women for only 2 spots. The interview is therefore between the three Marketing women: Hana, Izzy and Jade.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Farid, Gus, Hana, Izzy and Jade

title: Truth Teller Trio
stem:
Three colleagues — Anya, Bri and Cal — are each either a truth-teller (always tells the truth) or a liar (always lies). Each makes exactly one statement:

Anya: 'Bri is a liar.'
Bri: 'Cal is a truth-teller.'
Cal: 'Anya and I are both truth-tellers.'

How many of the three are liars?
answer_reason: Suppose Cal is a truth-teller. His statement would mean Anya is also a truth-teller. Then Anya's 'Bri is a liar' is true, making Bri a liar. But Bri's 'Cal is a truth-teller' would be true — a liar cannot say something true. Contradiction. So Cal is a liar. Bri's claim that Cal is a truth-teller is then false, so Bri is a liar. Anya's claim that Bri is a liar is true, so Anya is a truth-teller. Two liars: Bri and Cal.

title: Single-Use Coffee Cup Ban
stem: Should single-use coffee cups be banned in UK cafés to reduce landfill waste?
answer_reason: A links the action (banning single-use coffee cups) directly to the outcome (reducing landfill waste) with specific evidence. B is opinion-based and does not address landfill waste. C addresses café operating costs, not landfill. D restates general concerns without evidence and does not justify keeping the cups. A is the strongest.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; Environment Agency audits estimate that single-use coffee cups account for roughly 2.5 billion items reaching UK landfill annually, and switching cafés to reusable cups would eliminate this stream directly.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many customers say ceramic cups feel nicer to drink from.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some small cafés would struggle with the washing-up costs and staffing needed for reusable cups.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; the government should focus on bigger sources of landfill rather than coffee cups.

title: Compulsory Modern Languages
stem: Should pupils in English secondary schools be required to study a modern foreign language until age 16 to improve their later employability?
answer_reason: B connects the action (compulsory language study to age 16) to the outcome (later employability) with specific evidence from employers. A mixes European practice with pupil happiness — doesn't address employability. C addresses exam pressure, not employability. D is a sweeping generalisation with no evidence. B is the strongest.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; most European countries already require it, and pupils in those countries tend to be happier in school.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a 2021 CBI employer survey found 73% of UK firms rate candidates with a second language more highly in hiring, so extending compulsory study to age 16 gives more school leavers this advantage.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; pupils are already under exam pressure and adding another compulsory subject would worsen stress.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; many jobs in the UK can be done in English alone.

title: Screen-Based Homework Cap
stem: Should schools cap daily screen-based homework at 30 minutes for primary-school pupils to improve children's sleep quality?
answer_reason: A links the action (capping screen homework) to the outcome (sleep quality) with a specific evidence-based mechanism (evening screen exposure delays sleep onset). B is opinion rather than evidence. C is about marking convenience, not sleep. D addresses digital familiarity, which is not the outcome in the proposition. A is strongest.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; recent studies have linked more than 60 minutes of evening screen use in children to falling asleep over 45 minutes later on average, so capping screen homework at 30 minutes directly reduces this evening exposure.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many parents already believe their children sleep better with less screen time.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; teachers would find it harder to mark work handed in on paper.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; reducing digital homework would slow children's familiarity with computers.

title: Free Bus Travel for Under-18s
stem: Should free bus travel be introduced for all under-18s in the UK to reduce the number of family car journeys?
answer_reason: B connects the action (free under-18 bus travel) to the outcome (fewer family car journeys) with pilot evidence showing the intended effect. A addresses fare affordability, not car journeys. C is a sweeping claim about geography. D is about bus emissions, a different outcome. B is strongest.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; teenagers often don't have money for bus fares, so paying is a barrier.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a Department for Transport pilot in Scotland found that offering free bus travel to under-22s cut car-based school runs by around 18%, so a UK-wide scheme is likely to produce a similar reduction.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; many families live too far from bus routes to benefit.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; buses emit carbon, so filling them with schoolchildren still pollutes.

title: Compulsory First Aid at Work
stem: Should basic first-aid training be compulsory for all new hires in high-risk industries to reduce workplace fatalities?
answer_reason: A links the action (compulsory first-aid training) directly to the outcome (fewer workplace fatalities) with Health and Safety Executive evidence. B is emotional reasoning. C addresses cost, not fatalities. D is tangential — prevention vs response — and does not undermine the link between training and survival after an incident. A is strongest.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; Health and Safety Executive data show workplaces where at least 50% of staff are first-aid trained record 30% fewer on-site fatalities from heart attacks and severe bleeds, so mandatory training in high-risk sectors directly addresses the leading causes of workplace death.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; it would make employees feel more confident and cared for at work.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; small firms in high-risk industries may struggle with the training costs.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; first-aid training only covers emergencies, not the prevention of accidents.

title: City Rainfall Figures
stem: The table shows the monthly rainfall (in millimetres) for four UK cities in four selected months of a recent year.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Cardiff had the highest rainfall of the four cities in every month shown.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Cardiff (145, 98, 82, 140) exceeds each of the other three cities' figures in every listed month.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Norwich's monthly rainfall will remain below 80 mm in every future month.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Extrapolation trap. The table shows past data only — it cannot justify a claim about future months.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Bristol received more rain in October than in January.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Bristol: 110 mm in October versus 95 mm in January. 110 > 95.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Leeds had the lowest rainfall of the four cities in July.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Leeds in July = 72 mm. Norwich in July = 55 mm, which is lower.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: More rainfall means wetter gardens in Norwich than in Cardiff.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Cardiff has more rainfall than Norwich each month shown. Besides, the table shows rainfall, not garden wetness — requires outside knowledge to link the two.

title: Faculty Exam Averages
stem: The table shows the mean end-of-year exam score (out of 100) for four university faculties in three consecutive years.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every faculty's mean score improved between 2023 and 2024.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Humanities 66.8 → 69.2, Sciences 70.5 → 73.1, Engineering 71.0 → 74.5, Arts 61.2 → 63.8 — all increase.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Sciences had the highest mean score in every year shown.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: In 2024 Engineering (74.5) exceeded Sciences (73.1), so Sciences was not highest that year.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Humanities' mean score rose by more than 5 points from 2022 to 2024.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 64.1 → 69.2 is a rise of 5.1, which is greater than 5.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Arts will score higher than Engineering in 2025.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Future-prediction trap. Cannot extrapolate 2025 from the given years. Arts is also well below Engineering in every year shown.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Engineering's score increased by more between 2023 and 2024 than Humanities' did over the same period.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Engineering rose by 3.5 (71.0 → 74.5); Humanities rose by 2.4 (66.8 → 69.2). 3.5 > 2.4.

title: Retail Confidence Theory
stem: Some economists argue for the 'retail confidence' theory: when household savings fall below a threshold, consumers reduce non-essential spending even if their incomes remain stable. Supporters point to a 2019 UK survey showing that 62% of households with savings below £500 reduced spending on holidays that year, compared with 24% of households with higher savings. Critics note that the survey also measured perception of future income, and that most low-saving households reported job insecurity, so lower spending could be explained by expected income loss rather than the savings level itself. Both sides agree that the 2019 data show an association between low savings and reduced non-essential spending.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Low household savings cause reduced non-essential spending.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage presents this as a theory. Critics offer an alternative explanation (job insecurity), so causation is not established.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: The 2019 survey showed an association between low savings and reduced non-essential spending.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage explicitly states both supporters and critics agree on this association.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Most households with savings below £500 reduced their holiday spending in 2019.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 62% did, which is a majority — 'most' in UCAT means more than 50%.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Critics of the retail confidence theory believe the 2019 data should be ignored.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage says critics offer an alternative explanation for the data — not that they dismiss or ignore it.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Households with savings above £500 reduced their holiday spending at a lower rate than households with savings below £500.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 24% (higher savings) is less than 62% (lower savings) — lower rate, directly comparable.

title: Shelter Animals
stem: A shelter houses 40 rescued animals: 24 dogs and the rest cats. Three quarters of the dogs have been microchipped. All cats have been microchipped, but none of the cats have had their vaccinations updated this year.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: More than half of the animals at the shelter are dogs.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 24 dogs out of 40 animals is 60%, which is greater than half.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every microchipped animal at the shelter is a dog.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: All 16 cats are also microchipped — microchipped animals include cats as well.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: At least six animals at the shelter have not been microchipped.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Three quarters of the 24 dogs microchipped = 18, so 6 dogs are not microchipped. All cats are microchipped, so exactly 6 animals overall are not microchipped — satisfying 'at least six'.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some dogs at the shelter have had their vaccinations updated this year.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The stem gives no information on dog vaccinations, so nothing can be concluded about them.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No cat at the shelter has had its vaccinations updated this year.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Directly stated — none of the cats have had their vaccinations updated this year.

title: Garden Plants
stem: In a garden, every rose bush is either white or pink, except for a few rare hybrid bushes that are yellow. All hedge plants are green, and most of the hedge plants are trimmed weekly. Only climbing plants grow above three metres in this garden.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A rose bush in the garden that is not pink must be either white or yellow.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every rose bush is white, pink, or a rare yellow hybrid. Not pink narrows the options to white or yellow.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A plant in the garden that is not a climbing plant cannot grow above three metres.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 'Only climbing plants grow above three metres' — contrapositive: if not climbing, then not above three metres.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every hedge plant is trimmed weekly.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: 'Most' hedge plants are trimmed weekly — in UCAT this means more than 50% but not necessarily all. Some may not be.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every green plant in the garden is a hedge plant.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. All hedge plants are green does not imply every green plant is a hedge. Other plants could also be green.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Any yellow plant in the garden must be a rare hybrid rose bush.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage says rare hybrid roses are yellow but does not say only these are yellow. Other plants in the garden could also be yellow — the passage is silent on their colours.

title: Amateur Festival Performers
stem:
A local talent collective tracks 80 registered performers at an amateur festival. 28 perform a solo act, 30 perform a duet act, and 22 perform a band act. 10 performers do both a solo and a duet, 8 do both a solo and a band, and 7 do both a duet and a band. 4 performers do all three kinds of act. 21 performers do none of these three.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies: 4 perform all three (the triple overlap) and 21 perform none (outside). Scan — B shows 7 in the centre — eliminate. D shows 15 outside — eliminate. Between A and C, check solo-and-duet only. The stem gives 10 who do both solo and duet; 4 of those also do the band set, so solo-and-duet only = 10 − 4 = 6. A shows 6 — correct. C shows 10 (the pair total, not the 'only' count) — eliminate. Answer: A.

title: Community Festival Workshops
stem:
The diagram shows 140 workshops offered at a community festival. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a workshop that is both outdoor and free entry, but is neither hands-on nor held in the afternoon?
answer_reason: The workshop must be inside Outdoor and Free entry, and outside Hands-on and Afternoon. Letter T is Outdoor-and-Afternoon — includes Afternoon, excluded. Letter U is Afternoon-and-Hands-on — includes two excluded categories. Letter V is Hands-on-and-Free-entry — includes Hands-on, excluded. Letter W is Outdoor-and-Free-entry, sitting outside both Afternoon and Hands-on — this matches. Answer: Letter W.

title: Museum Artefact Inventory
stem:
A museum catalogues 60 newly acquired artefacts. 40 have been inspected. 25 of the inspected artefacts have been photographed. 12 of the photographed artefacts have also been published online. Every photographed artefact was first inspected, and every online-published artefact was first photographed.

Which of the following diagrams is consistent with the data?
answer_reason: The premises nest the three categories: online is inside photographed is inside inspected. Outside = 60 − 40 = 20. Inspected-only ring = 40 − 25 = 15. Photographed-only ring (inspected and photographed but not online) = 25 − 12 = 13. Online (innermost) = 12. Scan — B shows 15 in the innermost region (online should be 12) — eliminate. C has 12 in the outermost ring and 15 in the innermost — the two are swapped. D shows 17 outside — but 60 − 40 = 20 must sit outside — eliminate. Answer: A.

title: Fleet Vehicle Checks
stem:
The diagram shows 180 fleet vehicles categorised by five operational checks. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a vehicle that has been insured and tracked but has not been sprayed, serviced, or inspected?
answer_reason: The vehicle must be in Insured and Tracked but outside Sprayed, Serviced, and Inspected. Letter T is Tracked alone — missing Insured. Letter V is Insured-and-Serviced — includes Serviced, excluded. Letter W is Insured-and-Inspected — includes Inspected, excluded. Letter X sits in both Insured and Tracked and outside the other three spokes. Answer: Letter X.

title: Used Car Advertisements
stem:
A used-car website lists 160 current advertisements. 40 advertise a diesel engine, 50 advertise a sunroof, 44 advertise air conditioning, and 30 advertise heated seats. 10 advertisements list both a diesel engine and a sunroof. 12 list both a sunroof and air conditioning. 8 list both air conditioning and heated seats. 26 advertisements list none of these four features.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies: 26 outside (no feature), plus the three stated pair overlaps. Scan — D shows 18 outside — eliminate. C shows 34 outside — eliminate. B shows 12 in the diesel-and-sunroof region, but the stem gives 10 there — eliminate. A shows 10 for diesel-and-sunroof, 12 for sunroof-and-air-conditioning, and 8 for air-conditioning-and-heated — matches the stem. Answer: A.

title: Conference Sessions
stem:
The diagram shows 200 sessions at a regional conference. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents an on-site workshop with catering provided?
answer_reason: The session must be inside On-site, Catering provided, and Workshop, and outside Presentation. Letter R is on-site, catering and presentation — the wrong category (presentation, not workshop). Letter S is on-site and catering only, with no workshop. Letter U is on-site and workshop but without catering. Letter T is on-site, catering and workshop — matches. Answer: Letter T.

title: Luggage Scanner Comparison
stem:
Two luggage scanners are tested at an airport. When a scanner is shown a bag containing a prohibited item, Scanner X correctly flags it 91 times out of 100 and Scanner Y correctly flags it 78 times out of 100. When the same bag is scanned 60 times in a row by each machine, Scanner X returns the same result 54 times and Scanner Y returns the same result 58 times.

Which statement best compares the two scanners?
answer_reason: Accuracy is how often the machine gives the correct result. Scanner X = 91/100 = 91%, Scanner Y = 78/100 = 78% — Scanner X is more accurate. Precision is how consistently the machine gives the same result. Scanner X = 54/60 ≈ 90%, Scanner Y = 58/60 ≈ 97% — Scanner Y is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Scanner X is both more accurate and more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: B

title: Two Hearts in a Row
stem:
A standard 52-card deck has four suits (spades, hearts, diamonds, clubs) of 13 cards each. Two cards are drawn in succession from a shuffled deck, without replacement.

What is the probability that both cards are hearts?
answer_reason: P(first heart) = 13/52 = 1/4. After one heart is removed, 12 hearts remain in 51 cards, so P(second heart | first heart) = 12/51 = 4/17. P(both hearts) = (1/4) × (4/17) = 4/68 = 1/17.

title: Rare Condition Screening
stem:
A rare condition affects 2 in every 1,000 people in a population. A screening test correctly identifies the condition 95% of the time when it is present, and correctly returns a negative result 90% of the time when the condition is absent. One person is chosen at random from the population and tests positive.

Approximately what is the probability that this person actually has the condition?
answer_reason: Imagine 10,000 people. 0.2% have the condition = 20 people; 9,980 do not. Of the 20, 95% test positive = 19 true positives. Of the 9,980, 10% test positive (since specificity is 90%) = 998 false positives. Total positives = 19 + 998 = 1,017. P(has condition | positive) = 19 / 1,017 ≈ 1.9%, roughly 2%. The test's apparent accuracy is dwarfed by the base rate — most positives are false positives.

title: Eight-Sided Spinner
stem:
A spinner has 8 equal segments numbered 1 to 8. It is spun twice, and each spin is independent of the other.

Given that the first spin lands on an even number, what is the probability that the second spin lands on a number greater than 6?
answer_reason: The two spins are independent, so the outcome of the first does not change the probability of the second. Numbers greater than 6 on the spinner are 7 and 8 — that is 2 out of 8 segments, so P(second > 6) = 2/8 = 1/4.

title: Biased Coin Triple
stem:
A coin is biased so that it lands heads with probability 0.6 and tails with probability 0.4. It is flipped three times, and each flip is independent.

What is the probability of getting heads on all three flips?
answer_reason: Independent events multiply: P(all three heads) = 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.216.

title: Depot Packages
stem: No package at the depot is released for delivery unless it has been weighed and labelled. All packages weighing more than 30 kg are marked 'bulky' on their label. Some packages weighing less than 5 kg are sent for next-day dispatch. No next-day dispatch package is marked 'bulky'.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A package that has been released for delivery must have been weighed.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: No package is released unless it has been weighed and labelled, so release requires both — every released package has been weighed.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every package marked 'bulky' weighs more than 30 kg.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. The premise says all >30 kg packages are marked bulky, not that only those are marked bulky. Other packages might also be marked bulky.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A package sent for next-day dispatch cannot weigh more than 30 kg.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Any package weighing more than 30 kg is marked bulky. No next-day dispatch package is marked bulky. So next-day dispatch packages cannot weigh more than 30 kg.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All packages weighing less than 5 kg are sent for next-day dispatch.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Quantifier shift. Only some light packages go for next-day dispatch, not all of them.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some packages at the depot have not been labelled.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises only tell us that unlabelled packages cannot be released. Packages still at the depot could all be labelled — we cannot deduce any are unlabelled.

title: Glimps and Florks
stem: All glimps are florks unless they have been tizzed. Every florky creature sings loudly. No creature that has been tizzed sings loudly. Some glimps have been tizzed.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every glimp that has not been tizzed sings loudly.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every creature that does not sing loudly has been tizzed.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises only say tizzed creatures do not sing loudly — not that every non-singing creature is tizzed. A non-florky, non-tizzed creature that happens not to sing loudly is not ruled out.

title: Teacher Certification
stem: An examination board certificate is necessary to register as a teacher. Registering as a teacher is sufficient to receive the mandatory pay uplift. If a teacher has taught for more than ten years, they are eligible for the long-service bonus. Some registered teachers receive charitable grants.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A person without an examination board certificate cannot register as a teacher.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every registered teacher receives the mandatory pay uplift.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every teacher who has taught for more than ten years receives the charitable grant.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: If a person has an examination board certificate, they are registered as a teacher.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The certificate is necessary, not sufficient. Someone can hold the certificate without having registered.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A teacher with exactly five years of teaching experience is eligible for the long-service bonus.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Eligibility is stated only for teachers with more than ten years. Five years does not meet that condition, and no other route to the bonus is given.

title: Croopnuts
stem: Edible croopnuts must have been ripened and shelled. Only ripened croopnuts turn deep orange. Every croopnut that has been shelled was collected from the north grove. Some north-grove croopnuts are bitter.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A deep-orange croopnut must have been ripened.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only ripened croopnuts turn deep orange — so deep orange requires ripening.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every edible croopnut was collected from the north grove.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Edible croopnuts must have been shelled. Every shelled croopnut comes from the north grove. So every edible croopnut comes from the north grove.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every ripened croopnut turns deep orange.

decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The stem only says some north-grove croopnuts are bitter. Bitter does not tell us about edibility — nothing licenses 'some edible'.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A croopnut not collected from the north grove cannot have been shelled.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every shelled croopnut comes from the north grove. Contrapositive: not from the north grove means not shelled.

title: Reserve Rangers
stem: All foresters in the reserve are licensed rangers. Most licensed rangers are first-aid trained. Only first-aid-trained personnel may operate the emergency radio. No volunteer in the reserve is a licensed ranger.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No forester is a volunteer.

decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only first-aid-trained personnel may operate the radio, so anyone not first-aid trained is excluded.
