decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only first-aid-trained personnel may operate the radio. Most rangers are first-aid trained — but not all, so some rangers cannot.

title: Race Finish Order
stem:
Five runners — Amira, Beck, Cyn, Desh, and Eli — finish a race. Cyn finishes first. Amira finishes ahead of Beck. Desh finishes immediately behind Amira. Eli does not finish last. Beck does not finish immediately next to Eli.

Which of the following finishing orders, from first to last, is consistent with all the constraints?
answer_reason: Cyn takes first, so Amira, Beck, Desh, Eli fill positions 2–5. Desh is immediately behind Amira, and Amira is ahead of Beck. Eli is not last, so Beck is last. If Amira were in 2, Desh would be in 3, Eli in 4, Beck in 5 — but Eli (4) and Beck (5) would be adjacent, violating the last rule. So Amira is in 3 and Desh in 4, forcing Eli into 2 and Beck into 5. The order is Cyn, Eli, Amira, Desh, Beck — option B.

title: Raffle Ticket Sales
stem:
In a charity raffle, five stall-holders sold a combined total of 240 raffle tickets. Amy sold twice as many as Ben. Carla sold 20 more than Ben. Dan sold the same number as Amy. Enid sold 10 fewer than Carla.

How many tickets did Ben sell?
answer_reason: Let Ben's total be x. Then Amy = 2x, Dan = 2x, Carla = x + 20, Enid = x + 10. Sum: x + 2x + 2x + (x+20) + (x+10) = 7x + 30 = 240, so 7x = 210 and x = 30. Ben sold 30.

title: Project Assignments
stem:
Four colleagues — Priya, Quinn, Rami, Soh — are each assigned to exactly one of the four projects Alpha, Beta, Gamma, and Delta. No two colleagues share a project. Priya is not on Alpha and not on Delta. Quinn is on Beta or Gamma. Rami is on Delta. If Quinn is on Beta, then Soh is on Delta.

Which of the following assignments is consistent with all the constraints?
answer_reason: Rami is fixed on Delta, so Soh is not on Delta, which means Quinn cannot be on Beta (that would force Soh onto Delta). So Quinn is on Gamma. Priya is not on Alpha or Delta and is left with Beta. Soh takes the remaining Alpha. Priya–Beta, Quinn–Gamma, Rami–Delta, Soh–Alpha — option B.

title: Lab Door Mystery
stem:
Four students — Wren, Xia, Yaz, Zed — each made a statement about who broke the lab door. Each student either always tells the truth or always lies. Exactly one student broke the door, and exactly one student is lying. Wren says: 'I did not break the door.' Xia says: 'I did not break the door.' Yaz says: 'Wren is lying.' Zed says: 'Xia is telling the truth.'

Who broke the lab door?
answer_reason: If Yaz is the liar, then Wren is truthful — Wren did not break it, and Xia truthfully did not break it. Zed truthfully confirms Xia. That leaves Zed as the only possible breaker, and the pattern is self-consistent. Test any other liar: if Wren lies then Wren broke it, but Yaz truthfully says Wren is lying — already two truths that rule out Wren's confession, so the chain fails on counts. If Xia lies, then Xia broke it, but Zed truthfully says Xia is telling the truth — contradiction. If Zed lies, Xia is actually lying too, breaking the one-liar rule. Only Zed works as the breaker.

title: Round Table Seats
stem:
Six friends — Ava, Bao, Cal, Dev, Eve, Fin — sit around a round table at six numbered seats 1–6 arranged clockwise. Ava sits at seat 1. Bao sits directly opposite Ava. Cal sits two seats clockwise from Bao. Dev sits immediately to Ava's right (clockwise). Eve sits directly opposite Dev.

Who sits at seat 6?
answer_reason: Opposite pairs at a six-seat round table are 1–4, 2–5, and 3–6. Ava at 1 puts Bao at 4. Two seats clockwise from Bao (4) is seat 6, so Cal is at 6. Dev immediately to Ava's right (clockwise from 1) is at seat 2. Eve directly opposite Dev (2) is at seat 5. Fin takes the remaining seat 3. Seat 6 is Cal.

title: Dinner Shift Schedule
stem:
A restaurant manager is scheduling five servers — Fen, Gita, Hari, Ira, Jon — across a five-hour dinner shift that starts at 6 pm. Each server covers exactly one one-hour slot (6 pm, 7 pm, 8 pm, 9 pm, or 10 pm), and no slot has more than one server. Fen covers the 7 pm slot. Gita covers an earlier slot than Ira. Hari covers the slot immediately before Jon. Jon covers the 10 pm slot.

Who covers the 6 pm slot?
answer_reason: Jon is at 10 pm and Hari is immediately before him, so Hari is at 9 pm. Fen is at 7 pm, leaving Gita and Ira in the 6 pm and 8 pm slots. Gita is earlier than Ira, so Gita is at 6 pm and Ira is at 8 pm. The 6 pm slot belongs to Gita.

title: Office Grid Seating
stem:
A 3 × 3 office grid has nine desks. Rows are labelled Row 1 (front), Row 2 (middle), Row 3 (back); columns are Left, Centre, Right. Six staff — Mia, Nia, Oli, Pat, Quin, Ravi — each occupy one desk; the other three desks are empty. Mia sits in Row 2, Centre. Nia sits directly in front of Mia in the same column. Oli sits in the same row as Mia, in the Left column. Ravi sits directly behind Oli. Pat sits in the same column as Nia, in Row 3. Quin sits in a corner desk in Row 1.

In which desk does Ravi sit?
answer_reason: Mia is at Row 2 Centre, and Nia — directly in front of her in the same column — is at Row 1 Centre. Oli shares Row 2 with Mia but in the Left column, so Oli is at Row 2 Left. Ravi is directly behind Oli, placing Ravi at Row 3 Left. Pat shares Nia's Centre column and is in Row 3, so Pat is at Row 3 Centre. Quin takes a Row 1 corner. Ravi's desk is Row 3, Left.

title: Sugary Drinks Warning Labels
stem: Should sugary soft drinks be required to carry prominent warning labels to reduce the rate of childhood obesity in the UK?
answer_reason: B connects the action (warning labels on sugary drinks) directly to the outcome (childhood obesity) with a specific trial showing reduced sugar consumption in primary-age children. A addresses parental knowledge rather than obesity rates. C uses speculative language ('might be ignored') without evidence. D deflects by citing other obesity factors instead of assessing whether the labels themselves help.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many parents are unsure whether fizzy drinks are unhealthy.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a 2022 trial of warning labels on sugary drinks in Chilean schools reduced total sugar consumption by primary-age children by 24%, directly lowering the leading dietary driver of childhood obesity.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; warning labels might be ignored by shoppers who have always bought the same drinks.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; childhood obesity also depends on exercise and genetics, which warning labels cannot change.

title: Primary Cooking Lessons
stem: Should primary schools in the UK introduce a compulsory weekly cooking lesson to improve pupils' long-term dietary choices?
answer_reason: B ties the action (compulsory cooking lessons) to the outcome (long-term dietary choices) with a five-year follow-up study showing measurable impact at age 16. A addresses enjoyment, not dietary choices. C relies on an assumption about home cooking and uses 'many' rather than all. D raises curriculum logistics, not the dietary outcome.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; children often enjoy hands-on lessons.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a five-year follow-up study of a UK cooking-lesson programme found that participating pupils were 31% more likely to eat a balanced diet at age 16 than non-participants, directly improving long-term dietary choices.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; many parents already teach their children to cook at home.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; schools do not have enough curriculum time for additional compulsory lessons.

title: 20 mph Residential Limit
stem: Should the UK government introduce a nationwide 20 mph speed limit on all residential streets to reduce child pedestrian injuries?
answer_reason: B links the action (20 mph limit) to the outcome (child pedestrian injuries) with a published injury-rate figure. A addresses driver perception, not injuries. C narrows the scope to quiet cul-de-sacs, ignoring residential streets more broadly. D is opinion-based and does not address injury outcomes.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; drivers already find 30 mph limits too fast in school zones.

decision_making_question_options.label: B

decision_making_question_options.label: C

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; some motorists would resent the change.

title: Single-use Cup Levy
stem: Should single-use takeaway cups be subject to a nationwide levy to reduce littering in urban parks?
answer_reason: B links the action (nationwide cup levy) to the outcome (park litter) with a measured 34% drop in discarded cups after a similar Irish levy. A addresses café branding rather than litter. C assumes a substitution effect without evidence and diverts to a different waste type. D addresses enforcement cost, not the litter outcome.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many cafés are keen to appear environmentally responsible.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a 25p levy introduced in Ireland led to a 34% reduction in discarded takeaway cups in Dublin's public parks within twelve months, directly cutting park litter.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; customers would simply switch to disposable plastic bottles, creating a different kind of waste.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; enforcing a levy in every urban area would require additional staff.

title: Four-day Working Week
stem: Should companies be required to offer all employees a four-day working week to improve employee mental health?
answer_reason: B connects the action (four-day working week) to the outcome (mental health) with a measured 33% reduction in burnout symptoms from a 2023 Icelandic trial. A is preference-based, not a mental-health claim. C addresses operational workload, not mental health. D deflects by raising other causes of mental-health issues, rather than assessing whether the policy itself would help.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many employees would welcome more time off.

decision_making_question_options.label: B

decision_making_question_options.label: C

decision_making_question_options.label: D

title: Library Visitors by Age

decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: January total is 420 + 610 + 380 + 290 = 1,700. March total is 520 + 700 + 450 + 340 = 2,010. March is higher.

title: Warm-up Illusion
stem: A medical journal article discusses the 'warm-up illusion' — a theory that athletes perceive themselves as faster after a structured warm-up, even when their measured sprint times are unchanged. Supporters of the theory cite small-scale surveys in which athletes rated themselves as quicker after warming up, although some independent trials have produced mixed results. Critics argue that the self-reported feeling of readiness is more relevant to competition performance than any measured change.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: After a structured warm-up, athletes' measured sprint times are definitely unchanged.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage frames the warm-up illusion as a theory, and notes that independent trials have produced mixed results. So the 'measured times unchanged' claim is not definitively established.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Critics of the theory consider athletes' self-reported feeling of readiness to be relevant to performance.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage explicitly says critics argue the self-reported feeling of readiness is more relevant to competition performance than any measured change.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A structured warm-up causes athletes to feel faster.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage presents this as the content of a theory with mixed supporting evidence, not as an established causal fact.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some independent trials of the warm-up illusion produced different results from the small-scale surveys.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage directly says independent trials have produced mixed results, which means they differ from the consistently positive surveys cited by supporters.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: The warm-up illusion has no effect on sprint performance.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage does not make this claim. The theory is about perception versus measurement, and critics even argue perception matters for performance.

title: Delivery Fleet
stem: A delivery company's fleet has 80 vehicles. 60 are vans and the rest are lorries. Two-thirds of the vans are electric. Every lorry runs on diesel. No electric vehicle uses the northern depot.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: There are exactly 40 electric vehicles in the fleet.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Two-thirds of the 60 vans are electric, which is 40 electric vans. Every lorry runs on diesel, so no lorry is electric. 40 electric vehicles in total.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All diesel vehicles in the fleet are lorries.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: One-third of the vans — 20 vehicles — are not electric. Those vans are not stated to be electric, and the only powertrains mentioned are diesel or electric by implication, so non-electric vans are diesel too. Diesel vehicles include these 20 vans as well as the 20 lorries.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every vehicle at the northern depot is a lorry.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only electric vehicles are barred from the northern depot. A non-electric van could still use the northern depot — the depot is not restricted to lorries.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: There are exactly 20 non-electric vans in the fleet.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The fleet has 60 vans. 40 are electric (two-thirds), leaving 60 − 40 = 20 non-electric vans.

title: Running Club Disciplines
stem:
A running club has 80 members. 34 members compete in road races, 35 in trail races, and 28 in track races. 14 members compete in both road and trail. 10 members compete in both road and track. 9 members compete in both trail and track. 5 members compete in all three disciplines. 11 members do not compete in any of the three disciplines.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies: 5 compete in all three (the centre) and 11 compete in none (outside). Scan — B shows 3 in the centre, eliminate B. C shows 13 outside, eliminate C. That leaves A and D. The stem says 14 compete in both road and trail, 5 of whom also do track, so road-and-trail only = 14 − 5 = 9. A shows 9 there. D shows 7 there — eliminate D. Answer: A.

title: Nurse Grades
stem:
A hospital employs 240 nurses. 200 of these nurses are on the respiratory ward roster. Every senior-grade nurse is on the respiratory ward roster. Every shift-lead nurse is a senior-grade nurse. There are 48 senior-grade nurses, 15 of whom are shift-leads.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Freebies: 15 shift-leads (the innermost count), and 240 − 200 = 40 nurses outside the ward roster entirely. Scan — B shows 25 outside, eliminate B. C shows 10 shift-leads, eliminate C. That leaves A and D. The senior-but-not-shift-lead count is 48 − 15 = 33. A shows 33 there; D shows 48 there — eliminate D. Answer: A.

title: Book Club Genres
stem:
A 50-member book club tracks three genre preferences. 22 members enjoy mystery, 20 enjoy science fiction, and 18 enjoy biography. 9 enjoy both mystery and science fiction. 7 enjoy both mystery and biography. 6 enjoy both science fiction and biography. 3 enjoy all three genres. 9 members enjoy none of the three genres.

Which of the following diagrams is consistent with the data?
answer_reason: Freebies: 3 members enjoy all three genres (the centre) and 9 enjoy none (outside). Scan — C shows 5 in the centre, eliminate C. B shows 13 outside, eliminate B. That leaves A and D. Each shape's regions must sum to one of the stated category totals — 22, 20, or 18. In A the three shape totals come out as 22, 20, and 18, matching exactly. In D two shape totals both come to 22, so there is no valid assignment that matches the three stated category totals. Answer: A.

title: Four Parties Considered
stem:
A polling agency asks 120 voters which of four political parties — A, B, C, D — they might consider supporting at the next election. Voters may list two parties together only if those parties share a political tradition (A with B, B with C, or C with D). 24 voters consider Party A only. 9 consider both A and B. 18 consider B only. 7 consider both B and C. 22 consider C only. 6 consider both C and D. 16 consider D only. 18 voters do not consider any of the four parties.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Every region in this question has a stated count, so all values are freebies. Scan the bridges first: A-and-B is 9, B-and-C is 7, C-and-D is 6. B shows 7 in the A-and-B bridge — eliminate B. The stem says 18 voters consider none, so outside is 18. D shows 22 outside — eliminate D. That leaves A and C. A-only is 24. C shows 20 there — eliminate C. A matches every value. Answer: A.

title: Café Themed Nights
stem:
A café runs four themed nights: jazz, poetry, comedy, and open-mic. Of 80 performers on the café's books: 15 perform at jazz only, 14 at poetry only, 16 at comedy only, and 12 at open-mic only. 4 perform at both jazz and poetry, 3 at both poetry and comedy, 5 at both comedy and open-mic, and 2 at both open-mic and jazz. 9 are not currently booked for any themed night.

Which of the following diagrams best represents the data?
answer_reason: Every region has a stated count, so all values are freebies. Scan the four only-regions — jazz 15, poetry 14, comedy 16, open-mic 12. B shows 13 for jazz only, eliminate B. Outside is 9 performers. C shows 11 outside, eliminate C. That leaves A and D. Jazz-and-poetry is 4 and open-mic-and-jazz is 2. D shows 2 for jazz-and-poetry and 4 for open-mic-and-jazz — the two adjacent pair counts are swapped. Eliminate D. A matches every value. Answer: A.

title: Clinic Appointments by Team
stem:
The diagram shows 400 clinic appointments at a university health service. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents an appointment that was booked online and handled by the Mental Health team?
answer_reason: The question wants booked online AND Mental Health. Letter A sits inside booked online only — no Mental Health team. Letter B is General Practice only — not booked online, wrong team. Letter F is the overlap between booked online and General Practice — wrong team. Letter G is the lens where booked online overlaps Mental Health — that is the region. Answer: Letter G.

title: Summer Course Stages
stem:
The diagram shows 150 students progressing through a five-week university summer course. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a student who has completed the pre-reading and is attending lectures, but has not yet moved on to seminars or assessment?
answer_reason: The question wants pre-reading AND lectures, with nothing further. Letter F is the registered-and-pre-reading lens — no lectures yet. Letter H is the lectures-and-seminars lens — includes seminars, which is excluded. Letter C is lectures only — no pre-reading. Letter G is the lens where pre-reading overlaps lectures, with no seminars or assessment — that is the region. Answer: Letter G.

title: Music Streaming Playlists
stem:
The diagram shows 500 subscribers of a music streaming service. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a subscriber who has a premium plan and follows both the classical and the jazz playlists, but does not follow the rock, pop, or electronic playlist?
answer_reason: The question wants premium with classical and jazz, but none of rock, pop, or electronic. Letter B is premium with classical only — no jazz. Letter C is premium with jazz only — no classical. Letter H is the premium-jazz-rock region — rock is excluded. Letter G is the region inside premium where classical and jazz overlap with no other playlist — that is the region. Answer: Letter G.

title: Hospital Ward Rotations
stem:
The diagram shows 300 staff rotations at a hospital across six neighbouring wards. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a rotation that crosses between the cardiology ward and the renal ward only?
answer_reason: The question wants cardiology-and-renal only. Letter A is cardiology only — no renal. Letter H is renal-and-hepatology — wrong pair. Letter L is cardiology-and-rheumatology — wrong pair. Letter G is the lens where cardiology overlaps renal and no other ward — that is the region. Answer: Letter G.

title: Festival Volunteer Tasks

The diagram shows 300 festival volunteers categorised by the task areas they cover. Each letter marks a different region.

Which letter represents a volunteer who took on Registration and Merchandise, with no other task area?
answer_reason: The question wants Registration and Merchandise together, nothing else. Letter E is Merchandise only — missing Registration. Letter K is Registration with Cleanup — wrong specialist. Letter A is Registration only — missing Merchandise. Letter J is the lens where Registration overlaps Merchandise, outside every other role — that is the region. Answer: Letter J.

title: Two Reds With Replacement
stem:
A bag contains 12 balls: 5 red, 4 blue, and 3 green. A ball is drawn, its colour is noted, and it is put back in the bag. A second ball is then drawn.

What is the probability that both balls drawn are red?
answer_reason: With replacement, the two draws are independent and each has P(red) = 5/12. P(both red) = 5/12 × 5/12 = 25/144.

title: French and Spanish Conditional
stem:
A school has 200 students. 120 study French and 80 study Spanish. 50 students study both French and Spanish.

A student is chosen at random from those who study French. What is the probability that they also study Spanish?
answer_reason: Amongst the 120 French students, 50 also study Spanish. So P(Spanish | French) = 50/120 = 5/12.

title: Blood-Pressure Monitor Comparison
stem:
Two home blood-pressure monitors are tested. Monitor X gives readings within ±2 mmHg of the true value in 88 of 100 patients. Monitor Y gives readings within ±2 mmHg of the true value in 94 of 100 patients. When each monitor is used to re-test the same patient ten times, Monitor X produces the same reading on 8 occasions and Monitor Y produces the same reading on 5 occasions.

Which statement best compares the two monitors?
answer_reason: Accuracy is how often the reading is correct: X = 88%, Y = 94% — Y is more accurate. Precision is how consistent repeated readings are: X = 8/10 = 80%, Y = 5/10 = 50% — X is more precise. So Y is more accurate but X is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Monitor X is more accurate but Monitor Y is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Monitor Y is more accurate but Monitor X is more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Monitor Y is both more accurate and more precise.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Monitor X is both more accurate and more precise.

title: Rare-Condition Screening
stem:
A rare condition affects 1 in 500 people. A screening test correctly identifies the condition in 98% of affected individuals and correctly gives a negative result in 96% of unaffected individuals.

If a randomly chosen person tests positive, what is the approximate probability that they actually have the condition?
answer_reason: Imagine 10,000 people. 10,000 / 500 = 20 have the condition; 9,980 do not. True positives: 98% of 20 = about 20. False positives: 4% of 9,980 = about 399. Total positives = 20 + 399 = 419. P(condition | positive) = 20 / 419 ≈ 4.8%, roughly 5%.

title: At Least One Six
stem:
A fair six-sided die is rolled three times, and each roll is independent of the others.

What is the probability of getting at least one 6 in the three rolls?
answer_reason: Work with the complement: P(no 6 on one roll) = 5/6. P(no 6 in three rolls) = (5/6)^3 = 125/216. P(at least one 6) = 1 − 125/216 = 91/216.

title: Snurp Rings
stem: Only certified inspectors may stamp a snurp ring. Every stamped snurp ring is exported. No snurp ring may be exported without being weighed. Some certified inspectors are trainees.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every exported snurp ring has been weighed.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: No ring is exported without being weighed, so any exported ring must have been weighed.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A snurp ring stamped by a trainee would be exported.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Trainees are certified inspectors, so they are allowed to stamp. Every stamped ring is exported, regardless of who stamped it.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every weighed snurp ring has been stamped.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. Stamped rings must be weighed (since they are exported), but nothing says all weighed rings have been stamped.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No snurp ring stamped by a non-certified person exists.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Only certified inspectors may stamp a ring, so any stamped ring was stamped by a certified inspector.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some trainees have stamped snurp rings.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premises tell us trainees exist among certified inspectors, but not that any trainee has actually stamped a ring.

title: Hospital Keypads
stem: Having a valid staff ID is sufficient to pass through the ward keypad. A valid staff ID is not sufficient to enter the medicine room — both a valid staff ID and a separate medicine-room code are required. All doctors on shift have a valid staff ID. Some nurses do not have a valid staff ID.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every doctor on shift can pass through the ward keypad.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Doctors on shift have a valid staff ID, and a valid staff ID is sufficient to pass the ward keypad.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A nurse without a valid staff ID cannot enter the medicine room.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: A valid staff ID is required for the medicine room, so anyone without one cannot enter.

title: Cargo Permits
stem: No cargo container leaves the port unless sealed. Every container carrying hazardous goods must be sealed and labelled. Some containers at the port are labelled but empty. No empty container carries hazardous goods.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every labelled container at the port has been sealed.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Sealing is required only for containers that leave the port or carry hazardous goods. A labelled container still sitting at the port could be unsealed.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: An empty container that has left the port must have been sealed.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Nothing leaves the port unless sealed, so any container — empty or not — that has left must have been sealed.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some empty containers carry hazardous goods.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The premise states directly that no empty container carries hazardous goods.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every container carrying hazardous goods has left the port.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: We know hazardous containers are sealed and labelled, but the premises say nothing about whether they have been dispatched.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: No container carrying hazardous goods is empty.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: This is the contrapositive of 'no empty container carries hazardous goods' — they are logically equivalent.

title: Zorlins and Flimpets
stem: If a zorlin is ripe, it is sweet. Every flimpet is sweet. Some flimpets are zorlins. All unripe zorlins are bitter.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every ripe zorlin is sweet.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: This is the first premise stated directly.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every zorlin is either sweet or bitter.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: A zorlin is either ripe or unripe. Ripe zorlins are sweet; unripe zorlins are bitter. So every zorlin is sweet or bitter.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All flimpets are zorlins.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. We know some flimpets are zorlins, not all.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some sweet things are flimpets.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every flimpet is sweet, and flimpets exist (since some are zorlins). So at least some sweet things are flimpets.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every bitter zorlin is a flimpet.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every flimpet is sweet, so no flimpet can be bitter. A bitter zorlin therefore cannot be a flimpet, so this conclusion is false.

title: Cafe Pastries
stem: All pastries at the cafe are baked fresh. Some baked-fresh goods contain nuts. No nut-containing pastry may be sold to children. Only certified bakers can prepare baked-fresh goods.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A nut-containing pastry at the cafe may not be sold to children.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: No nut-containing pastry may be sold to children, so any such pastry at the cafe is excluded too.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every pastry at the cafe was prepared by a certified baker.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Every pastry is baked fresh; only certified bakers can prepare baked-fresh goods. So every cafe pastry was prepared by a certified baker.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Some pastries at the cafe contain nuts.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Some baked-fresh goods contain nuts, but the nut-containing ones could all be non-pastries — we cannot conclude any cafe pastry contains nuts.

title: Coach Licences
stem: No one may drive the coach unless they hold a PCV licence. All coach drivers are over 21. Every PCV holder has completed an eye test. Some people over 21 have not completed an eye test.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every coach driver has completed an eye test.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Coach drivers must hold a PCV licence. Every PCV holder has completed an eye test. So every coach driver has completed an eye test.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Every PCV holder is a coach driver.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. Coach drivers need a PCV licence, but PCV holders are not required to drive a coach.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Someone over 21 may be unable to drive the coach.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Some people over 21 have not completed an eye test, so they cannot hold a PCV licence and therefore cannot drive the coach.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Everyone who has completed an eye test holds a PCV licence.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: Reverse inference. PCV holders must have completed an eye test, but not all eye-test completers are PCV holders.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: A 20-year-old could be driving the coach.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: All coach drivers are over 21, so a 20-year-old cannot be driving the coach.

title: Bakery Loaves
stem:
Six customers (Alex, Bea, Cass, Dev, Ed, Fi) buy loaves at a bakery. In total they buy 30 loaves. Alex buys twice as many loaves as Bea. Bea buys one fewer loaf than Cass. Cass buys half as many loaves as Dev. Ed buys 5 loaves and Fi buys 4 loaves.

How many loaves does Dev buy?
answer_reason: Let Bea = x. Then Alex = 2x, Cass = x + 1, Dev = 2(x + 1) = 2x + 2. Ed and Fi contribute 9. Totals: 2x + x + (x + 1) + (2x + 2) + 9 = 30 → 6x + 12 = 30 → x = 3. So Dev = 2 × 4 = 8.

title: Seminar Rooms
stem:
Four seminars — Logic, Maths, Physics, and Biology — are running at the same time in four rooms in a row numbered 1 to 4 from left to right. Logic is not in Room 1. Maths and Physics are in adjacent rooms. Biology is immediately to the right of Maths. Physics is not in Room 4.

Which seminar is in Room 4?
answer_reason: Biology immediately right of Maths gives (Maths, Biology) on rooms (1,2), (2,3), or (3,4). Maths and Physics must be adjacent. If Maths = 1, Physics would need to be 2 but Biology is there — fails. If Maths = 3, Biology = 4 and Physics = 2, but Logic would then be in Room 1 — fails. So Maths = 2, Biology = 3, Physics = 1 (adjacent to Maths), and Logic = 4.

title: Three Friends, One Liar
stem:
Three friends — Hana, Ishan, and Jade — each make one statement. Exactly one of them is lying; the other two are telling the truth.

Hana says, 'Jade is lying.'
Ishan says, 'I am telling the truth.'
Jade says, 'Ishan is lying.'

Who is lying?
answer_reason: Test each case with exactly one liar. If Hana lies, Jade is truthful, so Jade's claim that Ishan lies is true — two liars, contradiction. If Ishan lies, Hana tells the truth, so Jade lies — again two liars. If Jade lies: Hana's claim that Jade lies is true, Ishan's claim that he tells the truth is true, and Jade's claim that Ishan lies is false. Consistent: only Jade lies.

title: Four-Floor Flat
stem:
A four-storey block of flats has one resident on each floor (ground, first, second, third): Nadia, Olaf, Priya, and Rafa. Nadia lives two floors above Priya. Olaf lives directly above Nadia.

Who lives on the ground floor?
answer_reason: Nadia is two floors above Priya: options are Priya on ground with Nadia on second, or Priya on first with Nadia on third. If Nadia is on the third floor, Olaf has no floor above — impossible. So Priya is on the ground floor, Nadia on the second, Olaf on the third, and Rafa on the first.

title: Disaster Response Team
stem:
A 16-person disaster response team will be drawn from four fire watches. The volunteers are listed below.

Watch Alpha: Paramedics — Maya, Sam; Engineers — Leo, Finn.
Watch Bravo: Paramedics — Ava, Nate; Engineers — Kai, Ezra.
Watch Charlie: Paramedics — Gus, Isla, Rhea; Engineers — Mae, Pia.
Watch Delta: Paramedics — Ben, Tess; Engineers — Ruby, Ola.

The team must contain exactly 4 members from each watch, with an equal split of paramedics and engineers. Where a watch has more volunteers than its quota in a role, a selection exercise decides who is chosen.

Which volunteers sit the selection exercise?
answer_reason: Each watch needs 2 paramedics and 2 engineers. Alpha, Bravo, and Delta each have exactly 2 of each — no selection needed. Charlie has 3 paramedics (Gus, Isla, Rhea) for 2 places, so those three sit the exercise. Charlie's two engineers (Mae, Pia) already fill the two engineer places.

title: Clinic Waiting Chairs
stem:
Six patients wait in a row of six chairs numbered 1 to 6 from left to right. The patients are Finn, Gita, Hugo, Isla, Jo, and Kai. Gita sits in chair 4. Hugo sits immediately to the left of Gita. Kai sits three chairs to the left of Jo. Finn sits in chair 6.

Who sits in chair 5?
answer_reason: Gita is in chair 4 and Hugo is immediately to her left in chair 3. Finn is in chair 6. That leaves Isla, Jo, and Kai for chairs 1, 2, and 5. Kai is three chairs left of Jo, so Kai = Jo − 3. The only possibility in the remaining chairs is Kai = 2, Jo = 5 — which leaves Isla in chair 1.

title: Vaping in Cars with Children
stem: Should vaping in cars carrying passengers under 18 be made illegal to reduce childhood asthma rates?
answer_reason: B directly connects the action (banning in-car vaping around under-18s) to the outcome (childhood asthma) with a specific NHS study. A uses 'many' and addresses parental choice rather than asthma. C raises enforcement difficulty without engaging with asthma. D is a comparative argument that sidesteps the asthma outcome entirely.

decision_making_question_options.label: A
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; many parents already choose not to vape in front of their children.

decision_making_question_options.label: B
decision_making_question_options.option_text: Yes; a 2023 NHS study found that second-hand vapour exposure in enclosed vehicles increases the risk of new-onset childhood asthma by 34%, so banning in-car vaping where children are present directly reduces asthma cases.

decision_making_question_options.label: C
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; the law would be difficult for police to enforce.

decision_making_question_options.label: D
decision_making_question_options.option_text: No; vaping produces less harmful residue than tobacco smoke.

title: Free Gym Memberships for Under-25s
stem: Should the UK government fund free gym memberships for all under-25s to reduce adult obesity rates in later life?
answer_reason: B ties the action (free gym memberships for under-25s) to the outcome (adult obesity rates) with a longitudinal study that tracks obesity at age 40. A cites enjoyment, not obesity. C narrows scope to 'many' and does not address obesity. D discusses cost and allocation, not the health outcome.

decision_making_question_options.label: A

title: Whale Song Passage
stem: Marine biologists have long studied how whale song changes over time. In many populations, all males in a given ocean basin sing nearly identical songs, which are updated gradually over several years. Occasionally a song from a neighbouring basin replaces the resident song across the entire population within a single breeding season — a phenomenon sometimes called a 'cultural revolution'. Most of the observations of this rapid replacement come from a single well-studied population off eastern Australia. While some researchers argue the pattern reflects rapid social learning, others caution that it may not generalise to all cetacean species.

decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage states that most observations of rapid song replacement come from the eastern Australian population, so it has been observed there.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Rapid social learning has been proven to be the mechanism behind these song changes.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage says 'some researchers argue' this — it is a proposed explanation, not a proven fact, and others urge caution.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: All cetacean species undergo rapid song replacement.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage explicitly notes the pattern may not generalise to all cetacean species.

decision_making_question_statements.statement_text: Whale song is updated more rapidly during a cultural revolution than under normal change.
decision_making_question_statements.answer_reason: The passage contrasts gradual change over several years with replacement within a single breeding season.

title: Glucose Meters
stem:

When each meter re-tests the same sample 40 times in succession, Meter X returns the same reading 32 times and Meter Y returns the same reading 38 times.

answer_reason: Accuracy is how often a reading is correct. Meter X = 90/100 = 90%, Meter Y = 80/100 = 80% — X is more accurate. Precision is how consistently repeated readings agree. Meter X = 32/40 = 80%, Meter Y = 38/40 = 95% — Y is more precise. So X is more accurate but Y is more precise.

title: Exactly Two Heads in Three Tosses
stem:
A fair coin is tossed three times. Each toss is independent.

What is the probability of getting exactly two heads?
answer_reason: There are 3 arrangements of exactly two heads in three tosses (HHT, HTH, THH). Each arrangement has probability (1/2)^3 = 1/8. Total = 3 × 1/8 = 3/8.

title: Two Blue Marbles
stem:
A bag contains 5 red marbles and 3 blue marbles. Two marbles are drawn at random, one after the other, without replacement.

What is the probability that both marbles are blue?
answer_reason: P(first blue) = 3/8. After drawing a blue, P(second blue) = 2/7. P(both blue) = 3/8 × 2/7 = 6/56 = 3/28.

title: Rare Disease Screening
stem:
A rare disease affects 2 in every 1,000 people. A screening test identifies the disease correctly in 98% of people who have it (sensitivity) and correctly rules it out in 94% of people who do not have it (specificity). A person is selected at random from the population and tests positive.

Approximately what is the probability that they actually have the disease?
answer_reason: Consider 100,000 people: 200 have the disease and 99,800 do not. True positives = 98% × 200 = 196. False positives = 6% × 99,800 = 5,988. Total positives = 6,184. Probability of disease given positive = 196 / 6,184 ≈ 3.2%.

title: At Least One Spade in Three Draws
stem:
A card is drawn at random from a standard 52-card deck and then replaced. This is done three times independently.

What is the probability of drawing at least one spade across the three draws?
answer_reason: Use the complement. P(not a spade on one draw) = 39/52 = 3/4. P(no spade in three independent draws) = (3/4)^3 = 27/64. P(at least one spade) = 1 − 27/64 = 37/64.

title: Passing at Least One Exam
stem:
The probability that a student passes the maths exam is 0.7. The probability that they pass the English exam is 0.8. The two events are independent.

What is the probability that the student passes at least one of the two exams?
answer_reason: Use the complement. P(fail maths) = 0.3, P(fail English) = 0.2. P(fail both) = 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06. P(pass at least one) = 1 − 0.06 = 0.94.
